mainEntity.name: Is a minor tooth chip something to be concerned about?

acceptedAnswer.text: A minor chip is a common dental occurrence and is not always a cause for immediate alarm. However, it is sensible to have any chip assessed by a dentist so that the extent of the damage can be evaluated. Some chips are entirely superficial and may be monitored over time, whilst others may benefit from prompt treatment such as bonding. The key is understanding what you are dealing with, which requires a clinical examination rather than an assumption based on appearance alone.

mainEntity.name: How long does dental bonding last on a chipped tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental bonding can be a durable solution, but it is not a permanent one. Longevity depends on several factors, including the size and location of the chip, the forces placed on the tooth during biting and chewing, and individual habits such as teeth grinding. On average, bonding may last several years before requiring maintenance or replacement. Your dentist can give you a more personalised indication based on your specific situation and dental history during a clinical consultation.

mainEntity.name: Can a chipped tooth get worse if left untreated?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, yes. A chip can become a site where plaque accumulates, increasing the risk of decay at that location. If the chip has created a rough or sharp edge, it may also cause soft tissue irritation over time. In less common cases, what appears to be a minor chip may have an associated crack that could propagate further under biting forces. This is one of the reasons why professional assessment is valuable — a dentist can identify any risk factors that might not be visible to the patient at home.

Dental bonding is generally a very comfortable procedure. In most cases, it does not require drilling or local anaesthetic, particularly for minor chips. The tooth is lightly conditioned, the resin is applied and shaped, and a curing light hardens the material. Many patients find the experience straightforward and comfortable. If there is any pre-existing sensitivity or if the chip is closer to the dentine, your dentist will discuss this with you beforehand and ensure you are comfortable throughout.

mainEntity.name: Is bonding a cosmetic or restorative treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental bonding can serve both purposes simultaneously, depending on the context. For a chipped tooth, it may restore structural integrity (restorative function) whilst also improving the appearance of the tooth (cosmetic function). In clinical practice, the two are not always strictly separated — a treatment that improves function often improves aesthetics as well. The primary purpose in your individual case would be discussed with your dentist, who will ensure any treatment recommended is clinically appropriate rather than purely cosmetic in intent.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my chip is affecting the dentine?

acceptedAnswer.text: You may not always be able to tell from appearance alone. Dentine involvement can sometimes be suggested by increased sensitivity — for example, discomfort when consuming something hot, cold, sweet, or when applying direct pressure to the area. However, not all chips into dentine cause immediate symptoms. A dental examination, which may include a gentle assessment of the tooth's response to stimuli, is the most reliable way to determine the depth of a chip and whether the underlying layers are affected.
